title: Executor Auth Strategies
subtitle: How OAuth, dynamic registration, MCP, and the CLI each mint one Connection
throughline: one credential — a Connection — born from whichever door the user walks through: OAuth, dynamic client registration, MCP, or the CLI bearer

chapters.title: The Connection Contract
chapters.blurb: Auth in Executor is a credential mechanism, not an integration type — and every strategy ends at the same shape: a Connection.

steps.title: The Connection Contract
steps.spoken: An integration is one thing. The credential that lets you call it is another. In Executor, auth is its own mechanism, and every strategy ends the same way.
steps.displayNarration: In Executor, **auth is a credential mechanism, not an integration type**. Every strategy converges on one shape: a `Connection`.

steps.title: Someone wants to connect
steps.spoken: It starts with a person who wants to connect an account. The thing that runs that connection is the OAuth service, with two methods: start, and complete.
steps.displayNarration: A user wants to connect an account. The flow is driven by **`OAuthService`** — just `start()` and `complete()`.

steps.title: The app is the OAuthClient
steps.spoken: The app itself is an OAuth client. It's pure identity: a client id, a secret, and its endpoints. It's owner scoped and integration independent, so one app can back connections across every integration that shares its provider.
steps.displayNarration: An **`OAuthClient`** is pure app identity — `clientId`, secret, and endpoints. *Owner-scoped* and integration-independent, so one app backs many integrations.

steps.title: Scopes are the integration's job
steps.spoken: The app deliberately doesn't carry scopes. What to request is the integration's concern, declared in its OAuth authentication template, keyed kind oauth2, alongside the scope list.
steps.displayNarration: The app carries no scopes. Each integration declares an **`OAuthAuthentication`** — `kind: "oauth2"` plus its `scopes` — which says *what to request*.

steps.title: Running the flow mints it
steps.spoken: Running that client's flow mints a connection. That connection is the credential: it records the owner, the integration, the auth template, and the backend provider, which for OAuth is simply oauth2.
steps.displayNarration: Running the flow **mints a `Connection`** — the credential. It records `owner`, `integration`, `template`, and `provider` (`OAUTH2_PROVIDER_KEY` = `"oauth2"`).

steps.title: Addressed for the tools
steps.spoken: Every connection gets an address, shaped tools dot integration dot owner dot name. That's the handle a tool call resolves later, when it actually needs the credential.
steps.displayNarration: Each `Connection` carries a **`ConnectionAddress`** — `tools.<integration>.<owner>.<name>` — the handle a tool resolves at call time.

steps.title: One shape, whatever the door
steps.spoken: So a person, an app, and a set of scopes go in, and one addressable connection comes out. Hold onto that shape. Every strategy in this book is just a different way to reach it.
steps.displayNarration: A user, an `OAuthClient`, and `OAuthAuthentication.scopes` in — one addressable **`Connection`** out. *Every strategy reaches the same shape.*

chapters.title: OAuth, Start to Connection
chapters.blurb: The authorization-code flow with PKCE: start mints a state, the user approves, and complete exchanges the code for tokens.

steps.title: OAuth, Start to Connection
steps.coverSubtitle: One call out, one redirect home
steps.spoken: The classic door is the authorization code flow. Let's walk one credential all the way through it, from the first call to the minted connection.
steps.displayNarration: The authorization-code flow with **PKCE**, end to end: `oauth.start` to `oauth.complete`.

steps.title: Start the flow
steps.spoken: You call start with the owner, the integration, and the auth template. The service takes it from there and begins building the round trip.
steps.displayNarration: **`oauth.start`** takes `owner`, `integration`, and `template`; `OAuthService` builds the trip and returns a `ConnectResult`.

steps.title: PKCE and a state token
steps.spoken: First it creates a PKCE code verifier and challenge, and a random state token. It stashes the state and the requested scopes in an oauth session row that lives just fifteen minutes.
steps.displayNarration: It mints a **PKCE** `createPkceCodeVerifier()` pair and a random `state`, persisting them with `requestedScopes` in `oauth_session`. TTL: `OAUTH2_SESSION_TTL_MS` = 15 min.

steps.title: Redirect to authorize
steps.spoken: Instead of connecting on the spot, the result is a redirect. It points the user's browser at the authorization server's authorize URL, carrying the code challenge.
steps.displayNarration: `ConnectResult` is `{ status: "redirect" }` — **`buildAuthorizationUrl`** points the browser at the AS `authorize` endpoint with the `code_challenge`.

steps.title: The code comes home
steps.spoken: The user approves at the provider. The authorization server redirects back to the oauth callback path, carrying an authorization code and that same state token.
steps.displayNarration: The user approves; the AS redirects to **`/oauth/callback`** with `code` and the original `state`.

steps.title: Complete reloads the session
steps.spoken: The callback hands off to complete. Complete looks up the session by its state token and reloads exactly the scopes that were requested when the flow began.
steps.displayNarration: **`oauth.complete`** takes `{ state, code }`, finds the `oauth_session` by `state`, and reloads its `requestedScopes`.

steps.title: Exchange, then mint
steps.spoken: Now it exchanges the code at the token endpoint, sending the PKCE verifier. Back come an access token and a refresh token, and from those it mints the connection, with provider oauth2.
steps.displayNarration: **`exchangeAuthorizationCode`** posts to the token endpoint with the verifier; the AS returns access + refresh tokens, and `mintOAuthConnection` writes the **`Connection`**.

steps.title: The whole round trip
steps.spoken: One call out, one redirect home, one exchange. State carried the flow safely across the browser, and the credential is now real.
steps.displayNarration: `start` → redirect → `/oauth/callback` → `complete` → exchange → **`Connection`**. The `state` token is the security gate across the browser hop.

chapters.title: No App? Register One
chapters.blurb: Dynamic client registration and MCP: probe a server, discover its metadata, register a public client, and bind tokens with a resource indicator.

steps.title: No App? Register One
steps.spoken: Sometimes there's no app to pick from a list, like when you connect a fresh MCP server. So Executor discovers and registers one on the fly.
steps.displayNarration: For MCP and other servers, **`oauth.probe`** discovers the endpoints and **`registerDynamicClient`** creates a client on the fly.

steps.title: Probe the protected resource
steps.spoken: You hand probe a server URL. It first fetches the protected resource metadata, the RFC nine seven two eight document, which names the resource and which authorization servers vouch for it.
steps.displayNarration: **`oauth.probe({ url })`** fetches the **RFC 9728** protected-resource metadata — the `resource` and its `authorization_servers`.

steps.title: Read the AS metadata
steps.spoken: From there it reaches the authorization server and reads its metadata, RFC eight four one four. That tells it the authorize endpoint, the token endpoint, and crucially whether dynamic registration is offered.
steps.displayNarration: It then reads the AS's **RFC 8414** metadata: `authorization_endpoint`, `token_endpoint`, and a `registration_endpoint` if dynamic registration is supported.

steps.title: Register a client
steps.spoken: If registration is offered, Executor posts its own client metadata to that endpoint, the RFC seven five nine one dynamic client registration call.
steps.displayNarration: **`registerDynamicClient`** POSTs client metadata to the `registration_endpoint` — **RFC 7591** Dynamic Client Registration.

steps.title: A public, secret-less client
steps.spoken: Back comes a client id with no secret. It's a public, PKCE-only client, and Executor stamps its origin as dynamic client registration so it's clear this app was born from a probe, not picked by hand.
steps.displayNarration: The AS returns a `client_id` with no secret — a public PKCE client. Its `OAuthClientOrigin` is `{ kind: "dynamic_client_registration" }`.

steps.title: Bind tokens to the resource
steps.spoken: One more thing makes this an MCP credential and not a generic one. The protected resource's URL rides along as an RFC eight seven oh seven resource indicator, pinning every token, even refreshed ones, to that exact server.
steps.displayNarration: The resource URL travels as an **RFC 8707** `resource` indicator on the client, so every `authorize`, `token`, and `refresh` request keeps the token bound to that MCP server.

steps.title: Discover, register, bind
steps.spoken: No app, no problem. Probe discovers, register mints a public client, and the resource indicator binds it. From here, the same authorization code flow from before carries it home to a connection.
steps.displayNarration: `probe` → AS metadata → `registerDynamicClient` → public **`OAuthClient`**, `resource`-bound. Then the *same* auth-code flow mints the `Connection`.

chapters.title: The CLI Door, and the Whole Picture
chapters.blurb: The CLI skips the browser with a bearer token from the environment — and every door, OAuth to CLI, ends at the same resolved Connection.

steps.title: The CLI Door, and the Whole Picture
steps.coverSubtitle: A bearer token, and one destination
steps.spoken: The simplest door skips the browser entirely. Then we'll pull back and see that every door we've opened leads to the very same place.
steps.displayNarration: The CLI authenticates with a plain **bearer token** from the environment — then a recap: every strategy ends at one `Connection`.

steps.title: Read a token from the env
steps.spoken: The command line tool reads a token straight from the environment. No redirect, no consent screen, no PKCE.
steps.displayNarration: The **`executor CLI`** reads `EXECUTOR_API_KEY` (or `EXECUTOR_AUTH_TOKEN`) from the environment — no browser hop.

steps.title: A stateless bearer
steps.spoken: If a token is present, read CLI server auth wraps it as a bearer and forwards it on every request. The CLI holds no credential of its own; it just carries the token through.
steps.displayNarration: **`readCliServerAuth`** returns `{ kind: "bearer", token }`, forwarded as `Authorization: Bearer …`. Stateless — no stored credential.

steps.title: Resolve the real Connection
steps.spoken: Authenticated, the server resolves the actual connection behind the request. This is the same connection the OAuth and MCP doors minted, addressed and stored exactly the same way.
steps.displayNarration: Authenticated, the server resolves the real **`Connection`** — the same credential the OAuth and DCR doors minted, with `expiresAt` and `oauthScope`.

steps.title: Resolved per invocation
steps.spoken: Each tool call resolves its connection lazily, by address, right when it's needed. The credential isn't passed around; it's looked up at the moment of use.
steps.displayNarration: Each **tool call** resolves its `Connection` lazily by `ConnectionAddress`, exactly when the tool runs.

steps.title: Quietly kept fresh
steps.spoken: For OAuth connections, when an access token nears expiry, within a sixty second skew, refresh access token quietly re-mints it in the background, and keeps the same resource binding intact.
steps.displayNarration: When a token nears expiry, **`shouldRefreshToken`** (skew `OAUTH2_REFRESH_SKEW_MS` = 60s) triggers **`refreshAccessToken`**, which re-mints it and keeps the `resource` bound.

steps.title: Four doors, one credential
steps.spoken: And that's the whole picture. OAuth, dynamic registration, MCP, and the CLI bearer are four different doors, but every one of them ends at the same resolved connection, ready for the next tool call.
steps.displayNarration: OAuth · DCR · MCP · CLI bearer — four doors, one **`Connection`**, resolved by address per tool invocation.
